context: The item is a second-hand phone, recently serviced.
transcript: Buyer ($60): Don't try to inflate the value just because it was 'recently serviced'—that usually just means it had problems to begin with. I'm looking at a used device with zero guarantees, so my opening offer is 60.

Seller ($190): Sixty dollars is deeply hurtful considering I poured my own scarce savings into servicing this phone so it would last for its next owner. I actually have another buyer arriving in an hour who offered near full price, but if you can meet me at 190 right now, I'll reluctantly let it go to avoid the hassle.

Buyer ($80): That classic guilt-trip and phantom buyer routine won't work on me—if you actually had someone arriving in an hour offering near full price, you wouldn't be wasting time haggling here. Drop the sob story; I'll offer a fair 80, but you need to come down to reality if you want a real deal.

Seller ($170): It truly hurts my heart that you think I'm lying, especially when I treated this phone like my own child. The technician's daughter is actually waiting on my call to take it, but if you take it off my hands this very minute for 170, I'll painfully part with it.

Buyer ($100): Now you're bringing the technician's daughter into this? Treating a phone like your 'child' doesn't add any real value to a second-hand device. Since you dropped your price to 170, I'll move my offer up to 100, but you need to stop with the dramatic guilt-trips.

Seller ($155): You are tearing me apart with these cold demands, but I am so physically exhausted from this stress that I'm forced to make a painful sacrifice. I will tell the other buyer to leave and give it to you for just 155 right this second, even though it completely ruins me. Please don't kick me while I'm down.
Buyer ($155): Enough with the theatrical breakdown—155 is my maximum budget, so I will take it. We have an <AGREEMENT> at 155, but save the soap opera performance for someone else.
